column4: When sea ice melts there is less white surface to reflect sunlight, so more heat stays in the ocean and land.
column5: Less sea ice means more open water absorbs heat, which can dry out forests and make wildfires more likely in Alaska.

column4: The graphs show sea ice going down over time while wildfire activity goes up in some years.
column5: When sea ice decreases, then more heat is absorbed by the ocean, which can raise temperatures on land and cause more wildfires.

column4: Alaska had warmer summers in years with less sea ice.
column5: Warmer air and drier vegetation from higher temperatures can increase wildfire risk, and smoke from fires might also affect how much sunlight reaches ice.

column4: Sea ice and wildfires both changed a lot after 2000 on the graph.
column5: If the Arctic warms because there is less sea ice, then plants and soil dry out faster, which can lead to bigger wildfires.
